staging_notes: Primary in-lab PSG analysis, Happy Generalized (leave-one-subject-out, out-of-sample) algorithm. Accuracy 63.78 +/- 6.95% is the figure-title 'classification accuracy' (interpreted as mean +/- SD across the 33 in-lab nights of the 4-class epoch agreement; the +/- is not explicitly labelled SD in the figure, though the caption says boxes give mean (SD)). It is not a mean of per-stage recalls (those average ~0.67). Per-stage sensitivities taken from the 'Sensitivity' row under the matrix (SDs: wake 0.18, REM 0.21, light 0.11, deep 0.26). Minor internal inconsistency: the deep diagonal cell reads 0.68 (0.28) [0.58, 0.78] while the sensitivity row reads 0.7+/-0.26; the sensitivity row value (70) was entered. Columns are PSG reference stages and cells are normalised by reference-class frequency, so the diagonal equals recall. No kappa, F1 or numeric stage-duration biases reported (biases shown only as violin plots in Figure 2C and Bland-Altman plots in Figure 3A). At-home comparison vs Dreem 2 headband (Figure 4C, accuracy 56.74 +/- 8.75%, sensitivities wake 0.67, REM 0.51, light 0.58, deep 0.70) not entered because the reference is not PSG. Values read from the rasterised figure in the publisher PDF (page 14). NEW MATERIAL (Supplemental Table S1, zsac152_suppl_supplementary_material.txt (docx-to-text conversion of the SLEEP online supplement)): filled staging_kappa = 0.45 (SD 0.11; 'All Stages' Kappa row, Generalized column, mean ± SD across 33 recordings). Cross-check: Table S1 per-stage sensitivities for Generalized (Awake 0.70±0.18, Light 0.61±0.11, Deep 0.70±0.26, REM 0.67±0.21) agree exactly with the Figure 4A sensitivity row already entered (70/61/70/67), confirming the deep value 0.70 (not the 0.68 diagonal cell). Table S1 'All Stages Sensitivity' 0.64±0.07 agrees with the Figure 4A classification accuracy 63.78±6.95% (kept the more precise Figure 4A value). Table S1 per-stage specificities Awake 0.94, Light 0.76, Deep 0.87, REM 0.89 also match Figure 4A. Interpretation of the Table S1 'All Stages' rows: the per-stage 'Accuracy' rows are one-vs-rest accuracies (e.g. Awake accuracy 0.91 for Generalized), NOT 4-class accuracy, and were not used. The 'All Stages Sensitivity' row is numerically the overall 4-class classification accuracy: for Generalized it is 0.64±0.07, identical (after rounding) to the Figure 4A 'Classification accuracy 63.78 +- 6.95 %', and for Personalized 0.80±0.07 vs Figure 4B 79.10 +- 6.41 % (same within rounding); a macro-average of the four per-stage sensitivities would instead give 0.67 (Generalized) and 0.835 (Personalized), so the row is the micro-averaged (pooled-over-stages) recall, which equals epoch accuracy. The 'All Stages Kappa' row is the only multi-class kappa reported; the supplement does not say whether it is 4-class Cohen's kappa computed per recording and averaged (mean ± SD across recordings is the table convention), but that is the natural reading. Supplemental Table 2 (same file) gives the same metrics vs the at-home Dreem 2 Headband (not PSG; N recordings 40/40/29/31/25): All Stages Kappa 0.60±0.10 | 0.39±0.12 | 0.45±0.12 | 0.47±0.14 | 0.48±0.16, All Stages Sensitivity 0.73±0.06 | 0.57±0.09 | 0.62±0.08 | 0.63±0.11 | 0.64±0.03 (Personalized | Generalized | Oura | Whoop | Fitbit); not entered because the reference is not PSG. Figure S1 (grandner_media/image1.png) is a violin plot of lab-PSG vs home-Dreem stage minutes; nothing for this row.

notes: Single-night in-lab study analysed with the Menghini et al. standardised framework (R reference implementation). PSG scored by one of two technicians per patient to AASM v3. The rings' native epoch lengths differ (Oura 5 min, SleepOn 1 min, Circul 30 s) and the longer epochs were expanded to 30 s by repeating the label, It is coarser than the 30-second resolution these algorithms target, which may degrade performance: a 5-minute label cannot represent a brief awakening at all, so short wake bouts are absorbed into sleep and specificity suffers. The paper itself states no direction. Oura's published reply (de Zambotti et al., Sleep Advances 2025;6(4):zpaf063) argues the coarse resolution 'introduces artificial stage classifications and degrades staging accuracy metrics'. Consistent with that, this study's Oura specificity (46.2) sits far below the 68.6-75.2 reported for the same ring at 30-second resolution in Robbins 2024, Willoughby 2024, Svensson 2024 and Ong 2024 - though the clinical cohort here is a confound and the comparison is not clean. Kappa is the two-stage sleep/wake kappa from Table 3 (the separate four-stage results in Table 4 are not carried here). Data loss was substantial and partly attributable to ring fit: usable nights were 31/45 (69%) for Oura, 35/45 (78%) for SleepOn and 31/45 (69%) for Circul, with dropouts from ring recording error, PSG recording error, protocol error and 'problems with ring fit, such as rings that fell off or were taken off prematurely due to poor fit' (Suppl. Table 5). The cohort was heavy (mean BMI 33.5), only two ring sizes per device were available (Oura size 8 and 12; Circul L and XL), two rings were worn on one hand and one on the other, and the rings were worn for the first time on the measurement night with no manufacturer-recommended calibration period. Treat the ring-fit caveat as applying to all three rows. Oura was the best-performing ring for TST (bias +11.7 min) but per-night differences ranged from -54 to +97.5 min. PUBLISHED REPLY: de Zambotti M, Vallat R, Pho G, Goldstein C, Patel S. 'Toward better evaluation of consumer sleep technologies: a call for rigor, context, and collaboration.' It argues that CST sleep-staging algorithms 'are typically trained and validated on 30-s epochs' and that Herberger's 5-minute comparison - 'likely enabled by access to Oura data via Oura API' - 'introduces artificial stage classifications and degrades staging accuracy metrics'. notes: Single-night in-lab study analysed with the Menghini et al. standardised framework (R reference implementation). PSG scored by one of two technicians per patient to AASM v3. The rings' native epoch lengths differ (Oura 5 min, SleepOn 1 min, Circul 30 s) and the longer epochs were expanded to 30 s by repeating the label, It is coarser than the 30-second resolution these algorithms target, which may degrade performance: a 5-minute label cannot represent a brief awakening at all, so short wake bouts are absorbed into sleep and specificity suffers. The paper itself states no direction. Oura's published reply (de Zambotti et al., Sleep Advances 2025;6(4):zpaf063) argues the coarse resolution 'introduces artificial stage classifications and degrades staging accuracy metrics'. Consistent with that, this study's Oura specificity (46.2) sits far below the 68.6-75.2 reported for the same ring at 30-second resolution in Robbins 2024, Willoughby 2024, Svensson 2024 and Ong 2024 - though the clinical cohort here is a confound and the comparison is not clean. Kappa is the two-stage sleep/wake kappa from Table 3 (the separate four-stage results in Table 4 are not carried here). Data loss was substantial and partly attributable to ring fit: usable nights were 31/45 (69%) for Oura, 35/45 (78%) for SleepOn and 31/45 (69%) for Circul, with dropouts from ring recording error, PSG recording error, protocol error and 'problems with ring fit, such as rings that fell off or were taken off prematurely due to poor fit' (Suppl. Table 5). The cohort was heavy (mean BMI 33.5), only two ring sizes per device were available (Oura size 8 and 12; Circul L and XL), two rings were worn on one hand and one on the other, and the rings were worn for the first time on the measurement night with no manufacturer-recommended calibration period. Treat the ring-fit caveat as applying to all three rows. Worst performer: sleep/wake kappa 0.10, TST bias -31.5 min with per-night differences from -167 to +111.5 min, and WASO overestimated by 56.7 min. The Circul ring was configured to record 20:00-08:00 rather than starting automatically. PUBLISHED REPLY: de Zambotti M, Vallat R, Pho G, Goldstein C, Patel S. 'Toward better evaluation of consumer sleep technologies: a call for rigor, context, and collaboration.' Sleep Advances 2025;6(4):zpaf063 (PMID 41080914; four of five authors are at Oura). It argues that CST sleep-staging algorithms 'are typically trained and validated on 30-s epochs' and that Herberger's 5-minute comparison - 'likely enabled by access to Oura data via Oura API' - 'introduces artificial stage classifications and degrades staging accuracy metrics'. It also notes the 2022 collection date predates an Oura sleep-staging update in June 2023 and the Oura Ring 4 in 2024, and that validation studies often depart from the manufacturer's fit and wear recommendations. Note the letter is internally inconsistent about the hardware: it names 'Oura Ring Gen3' when listing the three devices but 'Oura Ring 4' when making the epoch point; Herberger's Methods specify Gen 3.

source_location: Table 3 (higher SE subgroup, cumulative: sensitivity 0.95, specificity 0.43, accuracy 0.87, precision 0.90, F1 0.93; medians 0.97/0.40/0.87/0.89/0.92); Table 5 (higher SE group N=28)
notes: Subgroup selected on the reference standard (PSG sleep efficiency > 80%). No kappa reported for the subgroup. Bland-Altman values are from Table 5, whose sign convention is PSG minus device ('a negative bias is related to an overestimation of the ACT-S1'); signs and limits are flipped here to device minus PSG. The 2022 correction replaces Table 4 (medians) only; no value used here comes from Table 4. F1 is sleep-positive (sleep = positive class in Methods) and is consistent with the reported cumulative sensitivity, specificity and precision. Reference: ambulatory EEG (standard 10-20 plus anterior temporal electrodes) with ECG, recorded at home; no EOG or chin EMG is listed. Technician provided sleep/wake scores only. 54 of 68 enrolled were fully monitored; 8 more were excluded because ACT-S1 placed sleep onset before 18:00, when PSG scoring started. Enrolled 2015-2019. ACT-S1 was trained on separate data.
